newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Road through history to Afghanistan's frontline.
newsitem.headline: Road through history to Afghanistan's frontline.

text.p: The road from Kabul to Afghanistan's newest frontline is only 80 km (50 miles), but it is a journey through the timewarp of the country's recent past.

The Taleban, a purist Islamic movement which has overturned the stalemate of Afghan power politics with last month's lightning assault on the capital, has for the past few days directed its forces against the Panjsher valley.

Their target deep in the 150 km (100 mile) gorge is Ahmad Shah Masood, guerrilla general turned national military chief, who is pitting his wits and might against the Taleban who are now in control of more than three-quarters of the country.

For those watching this latest engagement in Afghanistan's long-running internecine conflict, it is a simple two-hour drive from Kabul to Golbahar, at the foot of the mountains that straddle the Panjsher valley.

Sharing the road, itself a partially finished monument to the Soviet occupation of the early 1980s, are heavily laden buses, herds of sheep and goats, the occasional ancient taxi, all of which make way for fast-moving jeeps and pickups ferrying heavily armed, turbanned Taleban warriors to the front.

Rocket-propelled grenades strapped to the sides, the jeeps flash past, cabins crammed with bearded Taleban while others cling to the back, Kalashnikovs strung over their shoulders. White flags, the chosen emblem of the Taleban signifying purity, flap from the aerials.
Beyond Kabul lie the plains of Koh Daman, a rolling valley of sand grey earth and hills overshadowed by the Cordaman mountains.

Along the road lie the ruins of mud walls, brick kilns and houses, all of them blasted as part of Soviet policy of depriving the mujahideen, Afghanistan's Islamic warriors, cover in their successful guerrilla campaign.
But in recent years much has been rebuilt, most of the buildings Afghan-style mud compounds with windowless outer walls.
Afghans wearing visors and flak jackets crouch among little flags and stone squares, painstakingly searching for mines that still litter the area.
At Jabal os-Siraj, or Mountain of Light, the road passes through groves of mulberry trees before turning to mud track, winding through the market to a fork in the road.
Straight ahead, the road climbs to the Hindu Kush and the Salang Tunnel, the entrance to provinces under the control of warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum.
To the right lie several miles of dust track and the Panjsher valley. As the road nears Golbahar, or Flowers of Spring, so does the war.
Rocket shell casings and their plastic containers litter the side of the road. At one point live shells have been lined up like bollards.

Drivers listen carefully, eyes warily scanning the mountain tops at the occasional sound of artillery, rocket or mortar fire. The road passes a former Soviet military base, a graveyard of tanks, artillery and trucks.

Golbahar itself, straddling the strikingly blue Panjsher river, is a ghost town. Only a handful of people remain, crouching in the shade watching plumes of smoke rising on the nearby mountain tops as Taleban hardware aims at Masood positions.

At the entrance to the gorge, wedged between sheer walls of rock, shells echo as they pass overhead. The occasional incoming mortar shell kicks up earth and dust, but the Taleban are used to it and barely move.

Warriors, some teenagers, straggle past in their usual garb of turban, traditional dress and informally strung Kalashnikovs. The road to the valley joins the river and is empty save the occasional goat, rocket launcher and abandoned tank. There is little else to indicate this is a war zone.
A passing Taleban suggests a visitor goes no further. The rumble of rockets exploding inside the canyon is persuasive.

Somewhere, deep inside the valley that has hosted two other great armies, Alexander the Great and Genghis Khan, lurk the forces of Masood, entrenched in a great natural defence of passes and overhanging rocks against the might of the Taleban.
